questions.prompt: Why is a compromised unconstrained-delegation host particularly dangerous?
options: It grants access only to a single, specific service
Domain Controllers periodically authenticate to such hosts, meaning the compromised host may hold a DC's own cached TGT
It only works against workstations, never servers
It requires krbtgt access to exploit at all
questions.explanation: DCs routinely authenticate to hosts with unconstrained delegation as part of normal operation — a compromised host can end up holding a DC's own TGT, a direct path to full domain compromise.

questions.prompt: What attribute does an attacker need write access to in order to stage a Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) attack?
questions.explanation: RBCD is configured via msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on the TARGET resource — write access to this attribute is the core prerequisite.

questions.prompt: Why does the default MachineAccountQuota value of 10 matter for RBCD specifically?
options: It has no relevance to RBCD
It means any domain user can create a machine account by default — exactly what's needed to control the account named in the delegation attribute
It limits how many times RBCD can be exploited per day
questions.explanation: Any domain user can create up to 10 machine accounts by default — giving a low-privilege attacker a controllable identity to name in the RBCD attribute, no credential theft required.

questions.prompt: What's the most direct mitigation that prevents RBCD abuse for standard users, rather than just detecting it?
options: Enabling BitLocker on all domain controllers
Reducing MachineAccountQuota to 0 for standard users
questions.explanation: Reducing MachineAccountQuota to 0 removes the prerequisite of being able to create an attacker-controlled machine account, closing off the RBCD path for standard users entirely.
